claims.text: Toughness retention in high-entropy alloys is governed by the nanoscale dispersion of coherently ordered precipitates.
Accelerated precipitate coarsening degrades toughness by forming preferential crack-initiation sites.
As-cast or rapidly solidified HEAs typically have an FCC or BCC structure and a nominally homogeneous elemental distribution.
Changing cooling rate can alter ordering kinetics and precipitate dispersion.
An approximately 2 at% Nb addition can alter ordering kinetics and precipitate dispersion.
Holding near 700°C below the order-disorder transition and then using slow cooling versus rapid quenching will produce different precipitate-size distributions.
TEM or APT can determine precipitate size, spatial distribution, and coherency.
A uniform nanoscale dispersion of coherent precipitates impedes crack propagation.
Coherent precipitates impede dislocation motion and crack nucleation.
Slow cooling or accelerated ordering kinetics causes precipitate coarsening.
Coarsened precipitates have a larger size and irregular distribution that act as stress concentrators.
Coarsened precipitates promote crack initiation and reduce toughness.
Samples with a fine, homogeneous nanoscale precipitate dispersion will have higher KIC than baseline samples.
Samples with coarsened precipitates will have reduced toughness and lower crack-initiation thresholds.
A standard rapid-quench treatment minimizes precipitate coarsening and produces a predominantly solid-solution microstructure with minimal ordered precipitates.
The proposed relationship applies to dominantly FCC or BCC HEAs processed from approximately 300°C to 800°C.
The proposed relationship may not apply to amorphous HEAs or systems with extreme secondary-alloying levels.
The relative contributions of precipitate volume fraction, size, and spatial distribution to toughness are not fully quantified.
Grain boundaries and other microstructural features may modify the precipitate–toughness relationship.
Failure to observe a statistically significant toughness reduction after verified precipitate coarsening would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome compares a fine precipitate dispersion against a rapid-quenched baseline described as having minimal ordered precipitates, while the experimental design separately says rapid quenching preserves a fine dispersion. Thus, the baseline mediator state is inconsistently defined.

The design calls for samples with identical base composition but also offers added Nb as the intervention; an Nb-added test sample is not compositionally identical to an unmodified control unless the heat-treatment-only and alloying experiments are explicitly separated.
